name: Gilit Mesopotamian Arabic
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: V. Akzent. Der bagdadische Dialekt weist folgende Akzentabweichungen vom Hocharabischen auf. Der Akzent rückt nicht über die drittletzte Silbe hinaus. Auf dieser liegt er nur dann, wenn die beiden letzten Silben offen sind: u̯älädi aber u̯äläd'nä. Wenn die paenultima geschlossen ist, liegt der Ton auf dieser Silbe: u̯äläd'kum; ḍuṛab'nä. Auf der ultima liegt der Ton, wenn sie doppelt geschlossen ist: šāfṓk sie haben dich gesehen. Ein Sproßvokal wird nicht betont: ríǧilhä; ḍuṛábitnä. Auch in Fällen, wo das auslautende h der dritten Person Mask. sing. nicht mehr gesprochen wird, bleibt der Ton auf der ultima: u̯ärā́ < u̯ärāh nach ihm; īdḗ < īdēh seine Hände; ġāḷbī́ < ġāḷbīh ihn besiegend (pl.). [Malaika 1963: 8] -- Jastrow 1980: 145: 'a) Fast überall läßt sich die heutige Betonung auf die ältere quantitative Regel zurückführen, nach der die erste Gruppe v̄K oder vKK vom Wortende aus gesehen betont ist, spätestens jedoch der drittletzte Vokal. Dieses Prinzip ist trotz unterschiedlicher Entwicklung der Silbenstruktur meist noch erkennbar: ... Bagdad-Muslime ḍúrbat »sie schlug«, ḍurbátni »sie schlug mich«.'
world_status: statement found in an open source

Auf dieser liegt er nur dann, wenn die beiden letzten Silben offen sind: u̯älädi aber u̯äläd'nä. Wenn die paenultima geschlossen ist, liegt der Ton auf dieser Silbe: u̯äläd'kum; ḍuṛab'nä. new_statements.translation: The Baghdad dialect shows the following accent deviations from Classical Arabic. The accent does not move back beyond the third-from-last syllable. It lies there only when the last two syllables are open: u̯älädi but u̯äläd'nä. When the penult is closed, the stress lies on that syllable: u̯äläd'kum; ḍuṛab'nä. The stress lies on the ultima when it is doubly closed: šāfōk 'they saw you'. An anaptyctic vowel is not stressed: ríǧilhä; ḍuṛábitnä. Also in cases where the final h of the 3rd person masc. sing. is no longer pronounced, the stress remains on the ultima: u̯ärā́ < u̯ärāh 'after him'; īdḗ < īdēh 'his hands'; ġāḷbī́ < ġāḷbīh 'defeating him (pl.)'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge, quantity-sensitive stress within a three-syllable window: a superheavy (CVVC/CVCC, 'doubly closed') final syllable is stressed; otherwise a heavy (closed or long) penult is stressed; otherwise the antepenult, never further back. Jastrow 1980:145 states the same for Mesopotamian Arabic generally as 'the first v̄C or vCC group counted from the word end is stressed, at the latest the third-from-last vowel' (Baghdad Muslim ḍúrbat 'she hit', ḍurbátni 'she hit me').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Malaika 1963 or Jastrow 1980.
new_statements.exceptions: Malaika: anaptyctic (Spross-) vowels are not stressed (ríǧilhä, ḍuṛábitnä) -- note Jastrow 1980:145 states the opposite for Muslim Baghdadi, that inserted vowels receive the stress before consonant-initial suffixes (čalíbkum, gaḷúbha, ḍurabítni, yuḍúrba); final stress persists where 3msg suffix -h has been lost (u̯ärā́ 'after him', īdḗ 'his hands'), giving stress-only contrasts (Jastrow: šā́faw 'they saw' vs šāfṓ 'they saw him'; wára vs wará 'behind (him)'); Jastrow: 3fsg -at often stressed before object suffixes (ḍúrbata ~ ḍurbáta); rural gilit (Šāwi, Kwairish) stresses the penult in CvCvCv(C) words where urban Baghdadi stresses the antepenult (Jastrow 1980:145; Meissner 1903:XIV).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms including suffixed words (pronominal/object suffixes count toward the window); Malaika frames the rules as deviations from the Classical Arabic accent, i.e. the CA-type weight rule is presupposed as baseline.
new_statements.identity_note: Quoted source (Malaika 1963) describes the Arabic dialect of Baghdad (Muslim Baghdadi), the reference variety of gilit Mesopotamian Arabic (meso1252; Glottolog has Baghdadi as a sub-variety). Corroborating source Jastrow 1980 covers all Mesopotamian dialects with explicit 'Bagdad-Muslime' (gilit) examples alongside qeltu points (Mardin etc., which belong to nort3142). Meissner 1903 describes the rural gilit dialect of Kwairish near Hilla; Van Ess 1917 is a pedagogical description of Basra/Baghdad speech. Khuzestani Arabic (Leitner 2022, Ingham) is also filed under meso1252 by Glottolog but was not accessible.

new_statements.relation_note: Same weight-sensitive, right-edge, three-syllable-window system as the catalog record from Malaika 1963 (closed penult stressed; 'doubly closed'/superheavy ultima stressed; antepenult only when the last two syllables are light); Erwin states it as one rightmost-heavy formula with a penult/antepenult default and adds the morphologically conditioned 'non-automatic' cases and the variable CvCvC-CV forms, which Malaika's paragraph does not list. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default ('automatic') stress falls on the rightmost heavy syllable, heavy = long vowel, or short vowel followed by two consonants or a geminate (so a final CVVC/CVCC and a closed penult attract stress, a plain final CVC does not); if the word has no such syllable, stress is penultimate in disyllables and antepenultimate in longer words (examples p. 40-41: šaafóo 'they saw him', náadi 'club', mádrasa 'school'). 'Non-automatic' stress (pp. 42-43) is morphologically conditioned: 2sg.m/1sg perfect forms stress the syllable before -it (darrásit), negative má-/lá- are usually stressed (má-yriid), interrogative š- puts stress on the first following vowel even if epenthetic (š-ítriid), prepositional prefixes b-/l-/mn- behave specially, and a few words in -aa; three-syllable CvCvC-CV(C) forms with a pronoun suffix vary between penult and antepenult (ibínha ~ íbinha).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress visible in the snippets
new_statements.exceptions: non-automatic stress classes A-G (perfect -it forms, negative and interrogative prefixes, prepositional prefixes, some words in -aa); variable stress in CvCuC-/CvCuCC- stems with pronoun suffixes; thereafter the book marks stress only in non-automatic cases A, B and G
new_statements.identity_note: Erwin 1963 describes colloquial Iraqi Arabic 'as spoken by educated Muslims in Baghdad' (ERIC ED012356 abstract; Muslim Baghdadi gilit), the same variety as Malaika 1963; Ingham 1974 describes the Arabic of Khuzistan (SW Iran), a rural gilit variety also under meso1252, not Baghdad.

new_statements.quote: Stress, the relative loudness or force of one syllable over others in the same word, is of two kinds in Iraqi. In the great majority of words, stress is determined by and can be predicted from the word's consonant-vowel structure; this is automatic stress. [...] 3.1 AUTOMATIC STRESS Automatic stress is predictable according to the automatic stress formula, as follows: Stress is on the syllable containing that long vowel, or short vowel followed by two consonants or a double consonant, which is nearest the end of the word; in the absence of such a vowel, stress is on the next-to-last syllable in two-syllable words and on the third-from-last in all others.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default ('automatic') stress is quantity-driven: stress the rightmost syllable whose vowel is long or is a short vowel followed by two consonants / a geminate (so final CVVC, CVCC and final long vowels take final stress: šaafóo 'they saw him', čaakúuč 'hammer', dazzéet 'I sent'; otherwise the last heavy: náadi, sallátha, mádrasa); if the word has no such syllable, stress is penultimate in disyllables and antepenultimate in longer words. Certain trisyllabic CvCuC(C)-+suffix words vary between penult and antepenult (íbinha ~ ibínha, ġúruftak ~ ġurúftak).

new_statements.identity_note: Erwin's object language is 'Iraqi' = the colloquial Arabic of Baghdad as used in the Georgetown Iraqi series (Muslim Baghdadi, i.e. the gilit variety that meso1252 'Gilit Mesopotamian Arabic' covers); the catalog record (Malaika 1963) is likewise the Baghdad dialect.

sources.quote: rules of stress assignment in HIA can be formulated taking into account the weight of the syllable and its position in the word. Hence we have the following rules: 1- Locate stress on the last syllable only if it is super-heavy / bis.'taan/ (orchard). 2- Locate stress on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy / tu.'faa.Ha/ (an apple) 3- Locate stress on the antepenultimate if both the final and the penultimate are light /' ka.ta.ba / (he wrote it) 4- stress may not retract beyond the antepenultimate.

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog arab1395). States that no Arabic dialect uses pitch for lexical contrasts (only some Arabic-based creoles have hybrid prosodic systems); Arabic dialects are stress-accent languages whose pitch events are intonational pitch accents and boundary tones, with cross-dialect variation in nuclear-contour inventory, head- vs edge-marking (Moroccan) and pitch accent density (Egyptian).
sources.venue: The Routledge Handbook of Arabic Sociolinguistics

tone.quote: No dialect of Arabic has yet been found which uses pitch to create lexical contrasts, though some Arabic creoles are reported to have hybrid prosodic systems (Gussenhoven, 2006). Comparative studies of intonation in Arabic are as yet relatively rare. Chahal (2006) provides a very useful overview, based on secondary analysis of a number of descriptions of a small number of dialects, and notes that the size of the reported inventory of nuclear tones appears to vary: some allow complex boundary tone combinations (such as a fall-rise, or rise-fall) and others display only simple contours (fall or rise)
tone.locator: author manuscript v0.2, section 5.2 'Intonational variation in Arabic', p. 11 (published chapter pp. 169-184)
tone.n_tones: None (no lexical tone in any Arabic dialect)

tone.quote: Since 'prosody' is not dealt with in any detail in this thesis, it is necessary to give, at this juncture, a breif account of 'accent' with reference to SIA. ... In SIA, the phonic features characterizing accentual prominence are: articulatory energy, melodic pitch and the perceived duration of the accented syllable. An accent in SIA (as in all languages or dialects) fulfils a contrastive function as it only "contributes to the individualization of the word or the unit which is characterized in contrast with the other units of the same type represented in the same utterance" (p. 83) ... It is also important to note that SIA has a 'free accent' ... In other words, the place of an accent in SIA is variable, i.e. it is not fixed to the same syllable in all SIA words.
